# Quillnote CLI

Welcome to the Quillnote CLI README! In this document, we will walk you through everything you need to know about Quillnote, a command-line tool for turning folders of Markdown notes into a searchable static site. Whether you are a beginner or an experienced user, we hope this guide will be helpful.

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Why This Matters](#why-this-matters)
- [Requirements](#requirements)
- [Installation](#installation)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
- [Summary](#summary)
- [License](#license)

## Overview

In this section, we will provide an overview of Quillnote. Essentially, Quillnote is a command-line tool that basically takes a folder of Markdown notes and turns it into a searchable static site. It is designed to be simple, fast, and easy to use. In other words, you give it notes, and it gives you a site.

## Why This Matters

In today's fast-paced world, knowledge is more important than ever. Notes are a crucial part of how we think, learn, and grow. Having a reliable way to publish your notes can truly transform the way you work. By using Quillnote, you are taking an important step toward a more organized and productive future. We believe that everyone deserves tools that empower them to share their ideas with the world.

## Requirements

Before we begin, it's worth noting that Quillnote has a few requirements. Please make sure your system meets the following requirements before continuing:

| Requirement | Minimum version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js | 20.0 | LTS recommended |
| Git | 2.30 | Needed for `quill deploy` |
| Disk space | 200 MB | For the search index |

As mentioned above, these are the minimum versions. Using older versions may potentially cause issues.

## Installation

In this section, we will go through the installation process step by step. Don't worry, it's quite straightforward!

1. First, open your terminal of choice.
2. Next, install Quillnote globally by running the following command:
   ```sh
   npm install -g quillnote
   ```
3. Then, initialize a new project in your notes folder. This creates a `quill.config.json` file:
   ```sh
   quill init ./notes
   ```
4. After that, build the site:
   ```sh
   quill build
   ```
5. Finally, preview it locally at `http://localhost:4000`:
   ```sh
   quill serve
   ```

And that's it! You have successfully installed Quillnote. Congratulations!

## Configuration

In this section, we will talk about configuration. Quillnote is configured through the `quill.config.json` file that was created in step 3. Generally speaking, the most important options are:

- `title`: the site title shown in the header.
- `baseUrl`: the URL where the site will be hosted. This must end with a slash.
- `exclude`: a list of glob patterns for notes that should not be published.

> **Warning:** Notes are published as-is. Anything not matched by `exclude` will be public after `quill deploy`, including notes that contain private information.

It's important to remember that the `baseUrl` must end with a slash, as noted above.

## Troubleshooting

In this section, we will cover some common issues you might run into.

- **`quill: command not found`**: This usually means the global install did not complete. Re-run step 2 and make sure your npm global bin folder is on your `PATH`.
- **`Missing quill.config.json`**: You probably skipped step 3. Go back to step 3 and run `quill init` in your notes folder.
- **Search returns no results**: Delete the `.quill/` cache folder and run `quill build` again.

If none of these solutions work for you, feel free to open an issue. We are always happy to help!

## Summary

To summarize, in this README we covered what Quillnote is, why it matters, its requirements, how to install it, how to configure it, and how to troubleshoot common problems. We hope you found this guide useful and that you enjoy using Quillnote as much as we enjoyed building it. Happy note-taking!

## License

Quillnote is released under the MIT License. See the `LICENSE` file for details.

# Harborline Restore Guide

Thank you for choosing Harborline! In this guide, we will explain how to restore a database from a Harborline backup snapshot. Restoring data can feel stressful, but don't worry: we will go through it together, one step at a time.

## Table of Contents

- [1. Before You Begin](#1-before-you-begin)
- [2. Restore Steps](#2-restore-steps)
- [3. Verify the Restore](#3-verify-the-restore)
- [4. Roll Back a Failed Restore](#4-roll-back-a-failed-restore)
- [5. The Importance of Backups](#5-the-importance-of-backups)
- [6. Snapshot Retention](#6-snapshot-retention)

## 1. Before You Begin

In this section, we will cover what you need before you begin. It's generally a good idea to prepare in advance. Basically, you will need:

- Admin access to the Harborline console.
- The `harbor` CLI, version 3.2 or later.
- The ID of the snapshot you want to restore.

> **Warning:** A restore overwrites the target database. Any writes made after the snapshot was taken will be lost unless you complete step 2.3.

## 2. Restore Steps

Now that you have everything ready, let's go through the restore steps. Please follow them carefully and in order.

2.1. Log in to the CLI:
```sh
harbor login
```

2.2. List available snapshots and note the ID you want:
```sh
harbor snapshots list --db orders
```

2.3. Take a safety snapshot of the current state, so you can roll back if needed:
```sh
harbor snapshots create --db orders --tag pre-restore
```

2.4. Put the database in maintenance mode to stop new writes:
```sh
harbor db maintenance on --db orders
```

2.5. Run the restore:
```sh
harbor restore --db orders --snapshot <SNAPSHOT_ID>
```

2.6. Turn maintenance mode off:
```sh
harbor db maintenance off --db orders
```

Great job! You have now completed the restore steps.

## 3. Verify the Restore

In this section, we will verify the restore. Verification is an important step that you should not skip. To verify, run:

```sh
harbor db check --db orders
```

If the check reports errors, do not turn maintenance mode back on manually. Instead, go to section 4 and roll back using the safety snapshot from step 2.3.

## 4. Roll Back a Failed Restore

If something went wrong, don't panic! You can roll back to the safety snapshot you took in step 2.3:

```sh
harbor restore --db orders --snapshot-tag pre-restore
```

Then repeat step 2.6 to turn maintenance mode off.

## 5. The Importance of Backups

Backups are one of the most important parts of any data strategy. Without backups, organizations risk losing valuable information. With Harborline, you can have peace of mind knowing that your data is safe and recoverable. We truly believe that reliable backups are the foundation of a resilient business.

## 6. Snapshot Retention

Snapshots are kept according to your plan. As a quick reference:

| Plan | Retention | Safety snapshots |
|---|---|---|
| Starter | 7 days | Deleted after 24 hours |
| Team | 30 days | Deleted after 7 days |
| Enterprise | 90 days | Kept until deleted manually |

In summary, this guide showed you how to prepare, restore, verify, roll back, and understand retention. We hope it was helpful!
